paragraphs.heading: What energy is
paragraphs.text: Energy is the measurable quantity that gets passed to a body or a system; we recognise it in the ability to do work and in heat and light. The word comes from the Ancient Greek energeia, meaning activity. Its SI unit is the joule, the energy spent when a force of one newton acts through one metre. Power is energy per unit of time, measured in watts, where one watt is one joule each second.

paragraphs.heading: Many forms
paragraphs.text: Energy shows up in many forms: the kinetic energy of a moving object, potential energy stored for example by an object's place in a field, elastic energy held in a solid, chemical energy, radiant energy carried by electromagnetic radiation, internal energy, and rest energy tied to mass. These forms overlap. Kinetic energy depends on motion, while potential energy reflects a capacity for motion, usually set by position in a field. Every form can be described as kinetic, potential or a mix, and some mixes get their own name, such as mechanical energy.

paragraphs.heading: Never lost, only changed
paragraphs.text: Energy is conserved: the total in an isolated system stays the same, even as it changes from one form to another. Noether's theorem explains why, tracing this law to physics having rules that stay the same as time passes. Theorists have understood the link since 1918.

paragraphs.heading: Energy and life
paragraphs.text: Every living thing is constantly taking in energy and giving it out. On a larger scale, Earth's climate and ecosystems run mainly on radiant energy from the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: From vis viva to energy
paragraphs.text: The ancient word energeia, which may first appear in the work of Aristotle, was a qualitative idea broad enough to cover happiness and pleasure. In the late 17th century Gottfried Leibniz proposed vis viva, or living force, the mass of an object times its velocity squared, and believed its total was conserved; today's kinetic energy differs from it only by a factor of two. In the early 18th century Émilie du Châtelet set out the idea of energy conservation in the margins of her French translation of Newton's Principia. Thomas Young may have been first to use the word energy in its modern sense, in 1807.

paragraphs.heading: Heat joins the picture
paragraphs.text: For some years people argued over whether heat was a substance, called caloric, or just a quantity like momentum. In 1845 James Prescott Joule found the link between mechanical work and the making of heat. These steps led to the theory of energy conservation, which William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, did most to formalise as thermodynamics.

paragraphs.heading: Mass is energy too
paragraphs.text: Albert Einstein's special relativity of 1905 showed that rest mass matches an equal amount of rest energy. So rest mass can turn into other forms such as kinetic or radiant energy, and back again, which means rest mass alone is not conserved while total mass and total energy are. Conservation of energy and conservation of mass turn out to be one law.
